notes:
I have gathered substantial material from four major commentaries (Guzik/Enduring Word, Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary, and Gill) plus excerpts from Hengstenberg, Constable, and others. I have reached search and fetch limits, so some tradition-specific sources (e.g., dedicated Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Catholic/Orthodox sites) could not be individually searched. Where those traditions are represented through the commentators I did access, I note it. Here are the verse-by-verse notes:

---

## Ezekiel 31 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1: *“In the eleventh year, on the first day of the third month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying,”*

- **Date:** The eleventh year of Zedekiah’s reign and Jeconiah’s captivity, on the first day of the third month (Sivan — roughly June 19, 587/586 B.C. by Bishop Usher’s reckoning). This was about seven weeks after the preceding oracle (Ezekiel 30:20–26) and only about **one month before the final fall of Jerusalem** (the Temple fell in the fourth month). (Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html; Guzik/Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **Prophetic timing:** The proximity to Jerusalem’s destruction makes the oracle pastorally urgent. Vawter and Hoppe (cited by Guzik) note that Ezekiel is helping Judah see its fate from a universal perspective — no nation escapes divine judgment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **Pulpit Commentary** dates it June 586 B.C., “two months all but six days” after Ezekiel 30:20–26. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-31.html)

### v. 2a: *“Son of man, say to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his multitude:”*

- **Addressee:** Pharaoh Hophra (Apries) and “his multitude” (Hebrew = *tumult*; the word connotes the noisy throng — troops, wealth, pride of every kind). Ezekiel, though in Babylon, is to address Egypt publicly as if in person. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm; Constable, excerpted via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-31.html)
- **Gill** adds: this is spoken not to Pharaoh personally by mouth (the prophet is in Chaldea) but by delivering a prophecy concerning him, which might be sent to Egypt. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)

### v. 2b: *“Who can be compared to your greatness?”*

- The rhetorical question functions like the opening of an Eastern parable (cf. Mark 4:30). It sharpens curiosity and draws in hearers. The question is repeated at the close (v. 18) to drive the lesson home. (Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-31.html; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **Gill:** “Look over all the records of time … draw a comparison between thyself and the greatest potentate that ever was; fancy thyself to be equal to him; this will not secure thee from ruin.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)

### v. 3: *“Look at Assyria, a cedar in Lebanon, with beautiful branches that shaded the forest. It towered on high; its top was among the clouds.”*

- **The parable’s subject — Assyria or Egypt?** Most commentators (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Guzik, Constable, Hengstenberg) hold that Assyria is the literal subject, used as an object lesson for Egypt. Some (Ewald, Cornill, Smend, and G.A. Cooke) emend the Hebrew *Asshur* to *te’ashshur* (“a fir/box-tree”) and read the whole parable as about Egypt. The Pulpit Commentary regards the traditional reading as more tenable. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-31.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **Why Assyria works:** Assyria had conquered Egypt and held it in vassalage, then had itself been conquered and annihilated only 37 years before this prophecy — by the same Chaldean power (Babylon) now about to judge Egypt. Egypt could not hope to resist the conqueror of her conqueror. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **“Top among the clouds”:** Most translators prefer “clouds” over “thick boughs” (so KJV margin, RV margin, Keil, Smend). The cedar’s top piercing the clouds suggests pride reaching toward heaven — an echo of Isaiah 14:14 (the Assyrian monarch attempting to ascend above the heights of the clouds). (Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-31.html; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **“Cedar in Lebanon”:** Lebanon is mentioned only because the most famous cedars grew there in perfection. Assyria did possess Lebanon at one period, but it was never its home. The “shadowing shroud” (KJV) vividly captures the peculiar foliage of the cedar. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm; Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-31.html)
- **Gill:** The Assyrian empire lasted from Nimrod’s times down to the recent past; the last king Saracus (or Chynilidanus) is probably in view. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)

### v. 4: *“The waters made it grow; the deep springs made it tall, directing their streams all around its base and sending their channels to all the trees of the field.”*

- **Waters = source of prosperity:** For Assyria, the waters represent the Tigris and Euphrates rivers with their trade and irrigation. For Egypt (the real target), the imagery fits the Nile with its canals and channels even better. (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/; Constable excerpts: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-31.html)
- **“The deep”** (Hebrew *tehom*) = the subterranean flood that nourished the tree. Ellicott notes this is the same concept as in v. 15 when God covers it in mourning. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **“Channels to all the trees of the field”:** The surrounding subordinate nations were nourished from the great stream of Assyrian prosperity. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The scenery is hardly that of Lebanon; it finds its counterpart in the Nile — and perhaps also the Tigris — with careful systems of irrigation. The cedar grows right by the river; other trees get only the smaller channels. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-31.html)
- **Gill** adds a secondary interpretation: “waters” and “the deep” may refer to the multitude of people that increased his kingdom (cf. Revelation 17:15). Targum: “by the people he was multiplied; by his auxiliaries he became strong.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)

### v. 5: *“Therefore it towered higher than all the trees of the field. Its branches multiplied, and its boughs grew long as it spread them out because of the abundant waters.”*

- The greatness described was the **direct result of God-given provision** (“the waters”). The height, the multiplied branches (provinces), and long boughs (extended reach) all flowed from divine supply — a fact that makes pride inexcusable. (Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html; Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **Hengstenberg** stresses: the greatness described in vv. 3–9 is glory *bestowed by God* on Assyria. (Excerpted in search results: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/heg/ezekiel-31.html)

### v. 6: *“All the birds of the air nested in its branches, and all the beasts of the field gave birth beneath its boughs; all the great nations lived in its shade.”*

- **A picture of imperial protection:** Birds, beasts, and “great nations” represent the many peoples who found shelter, stability, and prosperity under Assyrian (and Egyptian) rule. Cf. Ezekiel 17:23; Daniel 4:21; Matthew 13:32. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm; Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-31.html)
- **Gill:** Even people of “savage disposition” settled under Assyrian governance — built houses, planted vineyards, married, had children. The Targum: “in the shadow of his kingdom dwelt all the numerous people.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)
- **Guzik** notes that the description fits Egypt equally: before Jerusalem’s fall, many in Judah hoped to find protection under Egypt’s power. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)

### v. 7: *“It was beautiful in its greatness, in the length of its limbs, for its roots extended to abundant waters.”*

- **Beauty and stability combined:** Assyria was not only powerful but aesthetically magnificent (“beautiful in its greatness”). The secret of its beauty and reach was its root system — firmly fixed near abundant waters. (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **Pulpit Homiletics** draws a spiritual lesson: “The root lies low … the lordly branches could not thrive without the lowly root. Souls thrive on their humbler experiences. They grow strong in humility and trust … The root is unseen. It lies in dark underground regions.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-31.html)

### vv. 8–9: *“The cedars in the garden of God could not rival it … I made it beautiful with its many branches, the envy of all the trees of Eden, which were in the garden of God.”*

- **“Garden of God” / “Eden”:** This is not saying Assyria was *in* Eden (as Tyre was said to be in Eden, Ezekiel 28:13); rather, it compares the tree representing Assyria with even the trees of Paradise — and Assyria surpasses them. Yet the comparison may have been suggested by the fact that the traditional site of Eden lay within the bounds of the Assyrian Empire. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **“I made it beautiful”:** The pivotal theological statement. Yahweh himself declares that Assyria’s surpassing glory was his own work. As Block (cited by Guzik) puts it: “The great cedar’s glory is not of its own making; Yahweh has endowed it with the kind of superlative beauty that would evoke jealousy among all the other trees.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **Gill** on “envied him”: all the kings of the earth, though they dared not openly oppose, inwardly grieved at and grudged his grandeur superior to theirs. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)
- **The trees named:** “Fir trees” = cypresses; “chestnut trees” = plane trees (Ellicott). None in God’s garden could compare. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)

### v. 10: *“Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Since it became great in height and set its top among the clouds, and it grew proud on account of its height,’”*

- **The pivot from greatness to judgment.** The very greatness God bestowed became the occasion of sin. The heart “was lifted up in its height” — the sin of **pride**. As Matthew Poole (cited by Guzik) says: “His mind could no longer bear so great prosperity, he lifts up himself, and in his pride forgets God who lifted him up and will cast him down.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **Ellicott** explains the sudden shift to second person (“*thou* hast lifted up thyself”) as vividness in description; the third person returns afterward. The ground of judgment is pride — for which 2 Kings 18:32–35 (the Rabshakeh’s boasts) serves as a commentary. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **Hengstenberg:** “Greatness itself becomes a sin and a cause of the divine judgment, if it is not as it were expiated and sanctified by humble submission to God.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/heg/ezekiel-31.html)
- **Gill** notes the ambiguity: “because thou hast lifted up thyself” may address Pharaoh directly, or the Assyrian monarch by a change of person — both are guilty of the same pride. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)
- **Guzik** connects it to the Satanic impulse to pride seen earlier in Ezekiel 28:17. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)

### v. 11: *“I delivered it into the hand of the ruler of the nations, for him to deal with it according to its wickedness. I have banished it.”*

- **“Ruler of the nations” / “mighty one of the heathen”:** Identified as the Chaldean (Babylonian) monarch. At the time of Assyria’s fall, this was Nabopolassar (Nebuchadnezzar’s father). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm; Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **Gill** provides alternatives: some understand Arbaces the Mede (who defeated Sardanapalus); others Merodach-Baladan of Babylon (who vanquished Esarhaddon); but most likely Nebuchadnezzar (called Nabopolassar), who with Cyaxares of Media took Nineveh in the first year of his reign. Gill also notes some render it “into the hand of the god of the nations” — meaning the conqueror so called because of his great, divinely given power. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)
- **Ellicott** observes that here the prophet drops his figure to make a clear literal statement. The future tense is used poetically because the real object is Egypt, whose fall was still future. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **“I have banished it” / “driven him out”:** Hengstenberg sees an allusion to the driving of Adam from Paradise — also a consequence of pride, picking up the “garden of God” imagery from vv. 8–9. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/heg/ezekiel-31.html)

### v. 12: *“Foreigners, the most ruthless of the nations, cut it down and left it. Its branches have fallen on the mountains and in every valley; its boughs lay broken in all the earth’s ravines. And all the peoples of the earth left its shade and abandoned it.”*

- **“Foreigners … the most terrible of the nations”:** The Medes and the cruel Chaldeans (the soldiers of Babylon’s army). They are portrayed as “rough lumberjacks, who chop the tree down and leave it lying on the mountains.” (Guzik/Block: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/; Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)
- **The scattering of branches:** The provinces and tributaries broke off, revolted, or were seized by the conqueror — scattered “on the mountains and in all the valleys.” (Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)
- **“All the peoples … left its shade”:** Those who had sought protection now fled. Fair-weather allies desert in adversity. (Pulpit Homiletics: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-31.html; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **Clarke (cited by Guzik):** Nebuchadnezzar rendered himself master of Nineveh in the first year of his reign — about twenty years before Ezekiel delivered this prophecy. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)

### v. 13: *“All the birds of the air nested on its fallen trunk, and all the beasts of the field lived among its boughs.”*

- **Reversal of v. 6:** The birds that once nested in living branches now perch on the fallen ruin. The beasts that bore young beneath the shade now scavenge among the broken boughs. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **Ellicott:** There is no inconsistency between this and v. 12. At the fall all rush away to avoid the catastrophe; but as soon as the giant cedar is prostrate, they gather upon its trunk to fatten upon its ruin. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **Targum (cited by Gill):** understands it literally — the fowls and beasts feeding on the carcasses of the slain army: “upon the fall of his slain all the fowls of heaven have dwelt, and upon the carcasses of his army all the beasts of the field have rested.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)
- **Trapp (cited by Guzik):** “His dead body shall want decent burial, as afterward did great Alexander’s, great Pompey’s, our William the Conqueror’s, Richard III’s, etc.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)

### v. 14: *“This happened so that no other trees by the waters would become great in height and set their tops among the clouds, and no other well-watered trees would reach them in height. For they have all been consigned to death, to the depths of the earth, among the mortals who descend to the Pit.”*

- **The educative purpose of the judgment:** God felled Assyria so that other nations (“trees by the waters”) would take warning and not exalt themselves. The ultimate objective was to deter others from the same disastrous course. (Guzik/Feinberg: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/; Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)
- **“Stand up in their height”:** Margin reading “stand upon themselves for their height” — the thought is that princes shall no longer rely on their own strength and be infatuated by prosperity given them. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **“Consigned to death … descend to the Pit”:** Death is the great equalizer. All nations, like trees, eventually fall to oblivion like human corpses to dust. Sheol is the great leveller — “When it reaches the abode of the dead, Egypt must accept its solidarity with other, less important nations” (Vawter and Hoppe, cited by Guzik). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **Taylor (cited by Guzik):** “Death is the great equalizer and the surest antidote to an excess of ambition.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **Gill:** The end proposed is that kings of the earth — who rule over multitudes comparable to waters — should not be elated with pride … “for they are all delivered unto death … in the midst of the children of men, with those that go down to the pit”; in the grave they are on a level with the poorest of their subjects. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)

### v. 15: *“This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘On the day it was brought down to Sheol, I caused mourning. I covered the deep because of it; I held back its rivers; its abundant waters were restrained. I made Lebanon mourn for it, and all the trees of the field fainted because of it.’”*

- **Cosmic mourning:** The imagery shifts from a tree-felling to a funeral. God himself causes the mourning. “The deep” (*tehom* — the same flood that nourished the tree in v. 4) is covered as in mourning (the word “to mourn” is literally “to be black”). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **“I held back its rivers”:** God cuts off the water supply that made the tree great. For Egypt, this has reference to the many canals and waterworks fed from the Nile. When the Nile was low, these canals were restrained and agriculture suffered — a demonstration of God’s judgment (cf. Ezekiel 29:10; 30:12). (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **Lebanon mourns:** There is a subtle wordplay — Lebanon (*lebanon* = “white mountain”) is made to mourn (Hebrew root = “to be black”). (Guzik/Feinberg: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **“Trees of the field fainted”:** The subordinate potentates (other kings and nations) are dismayed at Assyria’s fall, just as in Ezekiel 26:15–18 the princes of the sea are dismayed at Tyre’s fall. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)

### v. 16: *“I made the nations quake at the sound of its downfall, when I cast it down to Sheol with those who descend to the Pit. Then all the trees of Eden, the choicest and best of Lebanon, all the well-watered trees, were consoled in the earth below.”*

- **Sheol shaken:** Like a great cedar crashing in Lebanon heard far away, the fall of Assyria reverberates among the nations — they shake with fear. (Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)
- **The dead consoled:** This echoes Isaiah 14:9–10, where the shades of the departed rise to greet the fallen king of Babylon. The “trees of Eden” (already-fallen great kings) are comforted to see that even mighty Assyria has joined them in the underworld. As Morgan (cited by Guzik) puts it: “The proud king is seen passing to Sheol … and the other fallen ones find satisfaction in that he too is brought low.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)
- **Block (cited by Guzik):** “No matter how high and mighty a tree may have been during its earthly existence, in death all are equal. The glorious cedar may have evoked jealousy in its earthly life (v. 9), but in Sheol it has nothing to be envied; all are on the same level.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **Gill:** “This is a poetic expression, representing the dead as rejoicing to see others in the same condition with themselves.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)

### v. 17: *“They too descended with it to Sheol, to those slain by the sword. As its allies they had lived in its shade among the nations.”*

- **Allies share the fate:** Those who were Assyria’s “arm” (its military strength, vassals, and allies) — who had lived in its shade — went down to Sheol with it, slain by the sword. Judgment sweeps in dependents as well as the principal power. (Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html; Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **Hengstenberg** notes that the allies who “sat in his shadow” are no help in the day of judgment; they share the fall. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/heg/ezekiel-31.html)

### v. 18: *“Who then is like you in glory and greatness among the trees of Eden? You also will be brought down to the depths of the earth to be with the trees of Eden. You will lie among the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword. This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD.”*

- **Direct application to Pharaoh:** The whole chapter is brought to a point. The opening question “Whom are you like?” (v. 2) is now answered: Egypt, like Assyria in glory, shall be like Assyria in judgment. The verse functions like Nathan’s “Thou art the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm; Pulpit: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-31.html)
- **“Among the uncircumcised”:** This is the deepest possible disgrace for Egypt. The Egyptians **practiced circumcision** and were meticulously careful about proper burial (as the pyramids attest). To be placed among the uncircumcised — barbarians outside the civilized world — was the ultimate humiliation. (Guzik/Smith/Feinberg: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/; Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-31.html)
- **“This is Pharaoh and all his multitude”:** The final identification. As Block says: “If he perceives himself as the heir of the Assyrians’ imperial might, then let him also share in their fate … the netherworld will reduce him to the lowest common denominator.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)
- **Gill** notes the Septuagint and Arabic render it: “So will be Pharaoh” — in like manner will he fall. The Targum reads “the wicked” for “the uncircumcised.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

Given search/fetch limits, I could not access dedicated pages from every tradition’s own sites. However, the commentators I did access represent several streams. Here is what could be discerned:

### Reformed / Presbyterian
- **Hengstenberg** (conservative Lutheran, widely used in Reformed circles) emphasizes that the greatness described in vv. 3–9 is *glory bestowed by God alone*, and that the fall is a direct outworking of divine sovereignty: “The greatness bestowed by God, being abused, is the cause of his fall.” He stresses the Adam-and-Eden typology (“I drove him out” echoes Genesis 3). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/heg/ezekiel-31.html)
- **Ligonier** resources (searched) recommend Daniel Block, Iain Duguid, and Derek Thomas as top Reformed commentaries on Ezekiel. Duguid especially offers “a very careful reading of the book from a Reformed perspective.” (https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/top-5-commentaries-ezekiel) — *Specific Ezekiel 31 content from these was not accessible within limits.*

### Baptist
- **John Gill** (18th-century Particular Baptist) provides a thoroughly predestinarian reading: God appointed the “mighty one of the nations,” God drove Assyria out, and the fall serves God’s educative purpose. His verse-by-verse notes are the most extensive traditional Baptist resource accessed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-31.html)
- **Guzik** (broadly evangelical/Baptist-leaning) provides a pastoral, application-oriented reading, emphasising that pride is the surest invitation to downfall and that God’s judgment on nations is universal. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
- **Enduring Word** (David Guzik) serves a broad charismatic/evangelical audience. Guzik’s application stresses the Satanic impulse to pride (linking v. 10 to Ezekiel 28:17) and the universal scope of divine judgment. No distinctly Pentecostal doctrinal distinctives (e.g., spiritual warfare readings of the “uncircumcised” as demonic) were found in the sources accessed. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/)

### Methodist / Wesleyan / Holiness
- **Adam Clarke** (Methodist) is cited several times by Guzik and referenced in the search results. Clarke stresses the educational purpose: “Let this ruin, fallen upon Egypt, teach all the nations that shall hear of it to be humble, because, however elevated, God can soon bring them down; and pride and arrogance, either in states or individuals, have the peculiar abhorrence of God. Pride does not suit the sons of men; it made devils of angels, and makes fiends of men.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-31/) — *Full Clarke commentary page was not accessible within limits.*

### Lutheran
- **Hengstenberg** (though shared with Reformed) represents the conservative Lutheran approach. His emphasis on divine sovereignty in both raising up and casting down nations aligns with Lutheran theology of the “two kingdoms” — God rules both. The specific LCMS and 1517.org sites were not accessible within limits.

### Anglican
- **Ellicott** (Anglican bishop) provides the classic moderate Anglican reading: careful philological notes, historical precision (noting Nabopolassar as Nebuchadnezzar’s father), and theological reserve. He highlights the difference between Assyria’s utter annihilation and Egypt’s prophesied continuance as a “base kingdom” (Ezekiel 29:14–15). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/31.htm)

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship
- **Text-critical issue in v. 3:** Some modern scholars (Ewald, Cornill, Smend) emend *Asshur* to *te’ashshur* (“a box-tree” or “fir-tree”), making the entire parable about Egypt, not Assyria. The Pulpit Commentary acknowledges this but rejects it. The NET Bible notes (not accessed within limits) likely address this. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-31.html)
- **Constable** (excerpted) notes that Allen (Ezekiel 20–48) “wrote an interesting paragraph on the motif of the cosmic tree in ancient mythology, which Ezekiel may have had in mind.” This reflects the comparative-religions approach of modern scholarship. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-31.html)
- **The “cosmic tree” motif:** Babylonian and Canaanite mythology featured a world-tree connecting heaven, earth, and the underworld. Ezekiel may be deliberately subverting this motif — the great tree is not a deity but a nation under Yahweh’s sovereign control.

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings
- **Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) and Orthodox (oca.org) sites were not accessible within search/fetch limits.** However, the traditional interpretation represented by the Church Fathers generally reads this as a literal prophecy against Egypt using Assyria as a type, with the “garden of God” / “trees of Eden” understood as the assembly of nations under God’s providence. The Fathers often draw moral applications about pride as the root of all falls.
- No uniquely Catholic or Orthodox doctrinal distinctives (e.g., purgatory, intercession for the dead) emerged in the sources accessed for this passage.

### Debated Popular Modern Teaching
- No prosperity-gospel, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace teachings on Ezekiel 31 were found in any accessed source. The chapter’s theme — the humbling of proud empires — is inherently antithetical to prosperity teaching. A prosperity reading would be unusual here.
